units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. If there's a crowd, a lot of phones, and a very small statue, you've found it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He stands at the corner of the Rue de l'Étuve and the Rue du Chêne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He's a bronze figure of a little boy, about fifty-five centimeters tall, relieving himself into a stone basin.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fifty-five centimeters. That's less than two feet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People are always surprised by how small he is.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Take a look at the setting. He's on a corner, on a wall, behind railings.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This isn't a monument in a grand square.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a street fountain that became a symbol.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How old is he?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first mention of a fountain figure of a boy goes back to the thirteen-hundreds.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bronze statue was made in 1619 by the Brabant sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And here's a detail that surprises people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The one you're looking at is a replica.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The original is kept in the Brussels City Museum, on the Grand Place, which is where we're going next.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why a replica?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Because he keeps getting stolen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Let me give you a few of the greatest hits.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A legend says English soldiers took him in the seventeen-forties, and he was found in a town called Geraardsbergen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The French grenadiers allegedly tried another theft in 1747.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Allegedly.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1817, a freed convict named Antoine Licas stole him and broke him into eleven pieces.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He was repaired and recast. In 1963 students from Antwerp hijacked him for five days.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the nineteen-sixties he disappeared again, after being broken, and divers recovered him from a canal in 1966.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A canal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Which is why there's a replica on the street, and the original is somewhere safe and dry.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What's the story? Why is a boy on a fountain doing that?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There are several legends, and nobody can prove any of them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The best known says that Duke Godfrey the Third of Leuven, a two-year-old, was hung in a basket from an oak tree to encourage his troops during a battle in 1142, and urinated on the enemy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A baby duke, doing military service.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Another says a boy put out a burning fuse that was meant to blow up the city walls.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Another says he put out a fire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Take your pick.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which one do I tell my friends?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The baby duke. It's the funniest.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's the wardrobe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the part I love. He has about a thousand costumes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The thousandth was presented in 2018.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They're changed regularly, for special occasions, for visiting delegations, for anniversaries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A little brass sign near the statue often tells you who he's dressed as today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A boy with a thousand outfits.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And they're all on display. Since 2017, there's a museum for them called GardeRobe MannekenPis, at number nineteen on the Rue du Chêne, just around the corner from where you're standing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Cute pun.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Garde-robe, wardrobe. Belgians like their puns.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What does this little statue tell me about Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That the city has always had a sense of humour about itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a capital of Europe with a famous symbol that's a boy doing a naughty thing, and everyone is fine with that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In fact they dress him up and give him a birthday.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And pause here. Stay a minute.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Watch the crowd.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Watch how people approach him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They all do exactly the same thing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They look, they laugh, they take a photo, and they leave.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. When you're ready, we head toward the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's only a few minutes away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Follow your map, or the crowds.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the way, you'll pass the Rue Charles Buls.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In it, there's a bronze monument to a man named Everard t'Serclaes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The one we should touch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. I'll tell you why when we get there.
